gadgets.versions: 7.x (measured live on 7.4.33, 2026-09-27). REMOVED in PHP 8.0, where an undefined constant is an Error.
gadgets.sink: any evaluator behind a character DENYLIST that leaves the parentheses and the ~ operator alone -- eval(), a calculator, an expression sandbox
gadgets.payload: a bare run of 0x80-0xFF bytes is an undefined CONSTANT, and PHP 7 evaluates it to its own name as a string. ~ complements it, so  ~(<bytes>)  is any ASCII string with no letters and no quotes in the request:  (~(\x8C\x86\x8C\x8B\x9A\x92))(~(\x9C\x9E\x8B\xDF\xD0\x99\x93\x9E\x98\xD5))  is  system('cat /flag*')
gadgets.effect: ONE byte of payload per byte of target string. The usual letter-free construction -- cut characters out of INF/NAN/scientific notation with string offsets and XOR them together -- costs roughly forty bytes per target character, which is what puts a correct payload over a length cap. Also: because the command string is built this way, the filter never sees its contents, so quotes, pipes, spaces and redirections are all available again inside it.
gadgets.precondition: PHP 7.x (check with a bare  _  : if it renders _ the fallback is live), and a filter that does not block the bytes 0x80-0xFF. A denylist written as [a-z'"] or [a-zA-Z] does not.
gadgets.trap: PHP identifiers accept 0x80-0xFF but NOT 0x00-0x7F punctuation, so the constant must be entirely high bytes -- you cannot mix in an ASCII character. A digit is fine after the first byte but not as the first. On PHP 8 this route is gone and the fallback is the INF/NAN plus XOR construction, which needs a much larger length budget. Note also that the same underscore probe that proves the version is itself a free 0x5F.

gadgets.sink: a filter that blocks both quote characters, leaving no string literal at all
gadgets.payload: (1/0) is the string INF, (0/0) is NAN, -(1/0) is -INF, (1/3) is 0.33333333333333 and (1/3)/(10**20) is 3.3333333333333E-21; concatenate with . and cut single bytes out with a string offset, e.g. ((0/0).(1))[1] is A
gadgets.effect: yields the bytes 0x30-0x39, 0x2B, 0x2D, 0x2E, 0x41, 0x45, 0x46, 0x49, 0x4E. The GF(2) span of those covers all of 0x00-0x7F, so every ASCII character is an XOR of at most four of them and any string can be built with no quotes and no letters.
gadgets.trap: (0/0)[1] yields nothing -- a float cannot be offset, so concatenate first. And concatenate with a PARENTHESISED digit: (0/0).1 is a parse error because .1 lexes as the float 0.1, while (0/0).(1) is the string NAN1. Budget about forty bytes per target character; on a length-capped input this is usually too expensive and the high-byte constant above is the answer.
